title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version emphasises the momentum form of Newton's second law and the impulse–momentum theorem with force–time graphs — the framing NEB theory questions use.

**Linear momentum:** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ — mass in motion, SI unit kg·m/s. It is a VECTOR along the velocity. A 1 kg ball at 10 m/s and a 10 kg cart at 1 m/s carry equal momentum but very different kinetic energies ($\frac{1}{2}mv^2$: 50 J vs 5 J).

**Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \dfrac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt}$. For constant mass this reduces to $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$ — but the momentum form is the GENERAL law and is the version that stays valid for variable-mass systems (rockets).

**Impulse:** $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\,\Delta t$ for a constant force, and $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt$ in general — the AREA under a force–time graph. Impulse has units N·s = kg·m/s, the same as momentum — by design.

**Impulse–momentum theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$. Any desired momentum change can be had with a LARGE force for a short time or a SMALL force for a long time — the product is what matters.

**Why airbags/crumple zones work:** to stop a passenger, $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash; extending the collision time $\Delta t$ cuts the average force $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$. Bending your knees on landing, catching a cricket ball with draw-back hands, and jumping with flexed legs are all the same physics.

**Worked example:** a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s. $\Delta p = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5$ kg·m/s → $F_{avg} = 45$ N. If caught in 0.02 s: 225 N — five times the force from the same momentum change.

**Variable force:** when $F(t)$ is a curve, impulse is the area under it; for $F = F_0 e^{-t/\tau}$-style impacts, $J = F_0\tau$. NEB usually gives triangular or rectangular force–time pulses — count the areas.

**NEB exam focus:** define momentum and impulse with units; state and use $F = dp/dt$; compute impulse from force–time graphs; apply $J = \Delta p$ to catches, kicks and landings; explain safety devices via the force–time argument.
confusion: ❌ 'Momentum and kinetic energy are interchangeable measures of motion.' ✅ Momentum $mv$ is a vector conserved in ALL collisions; kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is a scalar conserved only in elastic ones. Both grow with speed but differently.
❌ 'Impulse equals force.' ✅ Impulse = force × time (or the area under $F$–$t$). A small force acting long can deliver a huge impulse.

❌ 'The ball exerts no force on the bat while being hit because the bat is harder.' ✅ Newton's third law: contact forces are equal and opposite during the collision — the ball's velocity change comes from the contact force acting on IT.
❌ 'A heavy object always has more momentum.' ✅ Momentum = mass × VELOCITY — a light fast bullet can out-momentum a heavy slow trolley; direction matters too.
❌ Using $F = ma$ for a rocket ejecting fuel. ✅ Mass changes with time, so $F = ma$ fails; the momentum form $F = dp/dt$ handles it and yields the rocket equation.
❌ Impulse has units of newtons. ✅ N·s (= kg·m/s) — momentum units. Dimensionally $[MLT^{-1}]$.
practice: A 60 kg runner at 8 m/s is stopped in 0.5 s. Find the impulse and the average force. — $J = 480$ kg·m/s; $F = 960$ N.
A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 12 m/s and rebounds at 8 m/s. Find the impulse. — $\Delta p = 0.5(8+12) = 10$ kg·m/s BACKWARD (note the sign reversal!).
From a triangular $F$–$t$ pulse peaking at 400 N over 0.02 s, find the impulse delivered to a 0.2 kg ball at rest. — Area $= \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(400) = 4$ N·s → $v = 20$ m/s.
A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s crashes into a barrier that stops it in 0.4 s. Find the average force, and compare with a crumple-zone stop in 1.0 s. — 50 kN vs 20 kN.
A machine-gun fires 30 g bullets at 400 m/s, 10 per second. Find the average recoil force. — $F = n\,mv = 10 \times 12 = 120$ N.
universalFacts: Airbags, crumple zones, helmets and safety nets are all impulse engineering: stretch the stopping time, cut the peak force, keep $\Delta p$ fixed.
The impulse–momentum theorem explains why follow-through matters in sports — prolonging contact time increases delivered impulse and exit speed.
Rocketry is continuous impulse: each second, expelling mass $dm$ at exhaust speed $v_e$ gives thrust $v_e\,dm/dt$ — momentum conservation making spaceflight possible.
Karate masters break boards by maximising $\Delta p$ in minimum $\Delta t$: peak contact forces of thousands of newtons in a few milliseconds.
examples: Example 1 (recoil): a 5 kg rifle fires a 20 g bullet at 300 m/s — recoil speed $= \frac{0.02 \times 300}{5} = 1.2$ m/s backward.
Example 2 (kicking): a footballer gives a 0.45 kg ball at rest a speed of 20 m/s in 0.05 s — impulse 9 N·s, average force 180 N.
Example 3 (graph): a rectangular $F$–$t$ pulse of 250 N lasting 0.04 s delivers $J = 10$ N·s — a 2 kg cart leaves at 5 m/s.
Example 4 (safety): the same 4000 kg·m/s car momentum change stopped in 0.1 s (rigid wall) means 40 kN; in 0.5 s (crumple zone) only 8 kN — five times gentler.
Example 5 (jump landing): a 60 kg jumper hitting the ground at 6 m/s stops in 0.3 s with stiff legs (1200 N extra) vs 0.9 s with bent knees (400 N extra).
practiceQuestions: Q1. Define linear momentum and impulse, and state the relation between them.
Q2. Show that Newton's second law can be written as $F = dp/dt$ and state when this reduces to $F = ma$.
Q3. A 0.3 kg ball moving at 15 m/s is hit back along the same path at 25 m/s. Find the impulse delivered.
Q4. Explain, using the impulse–momentum theorem, why a crumple zone reduces injury in a crash.
Q5. From a given force–time graph (triangle), determine the final velocity of the struck body.
keyPoints: Momentum is a vector — always assign signs/directions before computing $\Delta p$.
Impulse and momentum share units (N·s = kg·m/s); impulse is the area under the force–time graph.
For a FIXED momentum change, force and time trade off: $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$.
$F = dp/dt$ is the general second law — essential for variable-mass (rocket) problems.
Momentum conservation holds in all collisions; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.
Recoil problems are momentum bookkeeping: $M V + m v = 0$ from rest.
summary: Linear momentum $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ measures 'quantity of motion'. Newton's second law in its general form is $\vec{F} = d\vec{p}/dt$, and integrating it over a collision interval gives the impulse–momentum theorem $\vec{J} = \int F\,dt = \Delta\vec{p}$ — impulse is the area under the force–time graph. Because a given momentum change can come from a big force briefly or a small force slowly, safety design (airbags, crumple zones, bent knees) is the art of stretching $\Delta t$. Recoil, ball games and rocket thrust are all direct applications.
specialNotes: Note 1: In rebound problems the velocity CHANGES SIGN — $\Delta p = m(v_f + v_i)$, not the difference. The commonest numerical error.
Note 2: Quote impulse in N·s and momentum in kg·m/s — numerically identical, and examiners check units.
Note 3: For force–time graphs, rectangular pulses are $F\Delta t$; triangular pulses are $\frac{1}{2}F_{max}\Delta t$.
Note 4: When a question says 'average force', it means $\Delta p/\Delta t$ — the constant force delivering the same impulse.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The linear momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity — a vector along the velocity.
Statement 2: The rate of change of momentum of a body equals the net force acting on it (general form of Newton's second law).
Statement 3: Impulse of a force is the product of the force and the time for which it acts, equal to the change in momentum produced.
Statement 4: For a fixed momentum change, the average force is inversely proportional to the collision time.
importantNotes: Note 1: Impulse units (N·s) and momentum units (kg·m/s) are identical — that is the theorem speaking.
Note 2: Momentum is directional: a rebound doubles the magnitude change versus a stop at the same speeds.
Note 3: The momentum form $F = dp/dt$ remains valid when mass varies (rockets, leaking trucks) where $F = ma$ fails.
Note 4: Force–time graph areas: rectangle = $F\Delta t$; triangle = $\frac{1}{2}F_{max}\Delta t$.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Rebounds: add the speeds in $\Delta p = m(v_f + v_i)$ — sign flip doubles the effect.
Trick 2: 'Soft landing' MCQs: longer $\Delta t$ ⇒ smaller $F$ ⇒ pick the option that stretches the time.
Trick 3: Recoil from rest: $V = mv/M$ instantly, with $V$ opposite the bullet.
Trick 4: Machine-gun/stream problems: average force = mass flow rate × exit speed ($n\,mv$).
Trick 5: If a force–time curve has no nice shape, the answer is still its AREA — estimate with boxes if needed.
examNotes: Exam Tip 1: Theory answers should state BOTH $J = F\Delta t$ and $J = \Delta p$ and connect them — one-line answers lose marks.
Exam Tip 2: In numericals, convert grams to kg and quote directions ('opposite to initial motion') with magnitudes.
Exam Tip 3: Graph-reading impulse questions: label the base and height you used to compute the area.
Exam Tip 4: Safety-device explanations score full marks only with the chain: fixed $\Delta p$ → longer $\Delta t$ → smaller $F_{avg}$.

importantConcepts: Concept 1: Momentum as the fundamental 'quantity of motion' vector $m\vec{v}$.
Concept 2: General second law $F = dp/dt$ and its constant-mass reduction.
Concept 3: Impulse as the time integral of force — area under $F$–$t$ — equal to momentum change.
Concept 4: Force–time trade-off: $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$ and safety engineering.
Concept 5: Recoil and variable-mass motion as momentum bookkeeping.
